extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys, agents, applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patentability (anticipation, obviousness, claim construction) of various claim types (process-of-use, product-by-process, apparatus, computer-implemented, Markush) under US law. Focused on how prior art, inherency, structure vs. function, and claim drafting affect rejections under 35 U.S.C. §§102/103 and §112.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency in anticipating method claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art device or reference may inherently perform a claimed method when used in its 'normal and usual operation'; a prima facie case of anticipation can be made on that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prior art structure inherently performs the claimed function (e.g., Donley inherently performs the function when used in ambient light), the examiner should explain that inherency. It is then up to the applicant to prove the prior art structure would not perform the claimed method when used normally. Examples: Donley/King (coated substrate inherent absorption/reflection), In re Best (cooling step inherent in handling Hansford's zeolite). Evidence comparing properties or showing a difference in operation could rebut the rejection; absence of such evidence supports anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of new uses of old structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of a new use for an old structure based on previously unknown properties might be patentable as a process of using, but if the claim is directed to a result/property of an old composition/structure, it may be anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law: In re Hack supports patentability of new uses; In re May holds claims directed to a result/property of old compounds were anticipated where prior art disclosed same compounds and a method for effecting the same result (even if silent on another property like addiction). The mere finding of a new property in an old composition is 'tantamount only to finding a property in the old composition' and may not render a new patentable use. Applicants should claim/processes directed to new compounds or show unexpected properties to avoid anticipation/obviousness rejections (see Tomlinson, May, and Tomlinson examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims judged by the product, not production steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-by-process claims are defined by the process in the claim, but patentability is determined based on the product itself; if the product is the same as or obvious from a prior art product, the product-by-process claim is unpatentable even if made by a different process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: In re Thorpe, Amgen v. Roche, Biogen v. EMD Serono, United Therapeutics v. Liquidia, Purdue Pharma v. Epic. Examiners should compare the claimed product to prior art products; if identical or obvious from prior art products, reject under 35 U.S.C. 102/103. Note: for infringement analysis, a product-by-process claim is infringed only by a product made by the recited process. The examiner should consider both anticipation and obviousness aspects when relying on prior art products made by different processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of structure implied by process steps for product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Process steps in a product-by-process claim can imply structural characteristics of the product; those implied structures should be considered when assessing patentability over prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the manufacturing process would be expected to impart structural characteristics to the final product, the implied structure can limit the claim (In re Garnero; In re Nordt Dev. Co.). Terms like 'interbonded by interfusion,' 'welded,' 'intermixed,' 'ground in place,' 'press fitted,' and 'etched' may be construed as structural limitations. Examiners should consider whether the process language conveys a structural limitation that distinguishes the product from prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shifts to applicant to show nonobvious difference for apparently identical products
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an examiner shows the claimed product appears the same or similar to a prior art product (even if made by a different process), the burden shifts to the applicant to present evidence of a nonobvious difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because prima facie obviousness for product-by-process claims is easier to make, applicants must provide evidence (e.g., compositional analysis, comparative data showing unexpected properties) that establishes a nonobvious difference between the claimed product and the prior art (In re Fessmann; In re Marosi; Ex parte Gray). If applicant offers only speculative assertions without concrete comparisons, the rejection will be upheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 rejections acceptable for product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior art discloses a product that reasonably appears identical or only slightly different from the claimed product, it is fair to reject product-by-process claims alternatively under §102 (anticipation) or §103 (obviousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the Patent Office cannot practicably manufacture and test every prior art product against each claimed product. Examiners relying on these alternative grounds must still explain both anticipation and obviousness aspects of the rejection (In re Brown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency and functional limitations in apparatus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a functional limitation in an apparatus claim is an inherent characteristic of prior art structure, the examiner should explain that the prior art inherently possesses the claimed functional limitation; the burden then shifts to the applicant to prove absence of that characteristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Schreiber, Bettcher v. Bunzl, In re Swinehart. Examiners should articulate why the prior art structure inherently meets the functional limitation. If there is reason to believe the functional limitation may be inherent, the Office may require the applicant to prove the prior art does not possess that characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of operating a device does not impart patentability to an apparatus claim
rubrics_metrics.description: An apparatus claim covers what a device is, not how it is used; reciting the intended manner of use (preamble recitation) does not differentiate the claim from prior art if the prior art teaches all structural limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Bausch & Lomb; Ex parte Masham. For example, a claim preamble stating 'for mixing flowing developer material' does not distinguish the apparatus if the prior art structure is the same despite differences in degree of submersion or intended use. Examiners should focus on structural elements rather than recited intended use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus that performs claimed functions may still not anticipate if structural difference exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a prior art device can perform all the functions recited in the claim, anticipation requires disclosure (express or inherent) of the claimed structure; a structural difference can prevent anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means-plus-function limitations are met only by structures equivalent to the corresponding structures in the specification (In re Donaldson). Example: a diaper reference disclosed two fastening elements that could perform the same function as three claimed elements, but the court required three separate elements (In re Robertson). Examiners must evaluate structural disclosure, not just functional capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented functional claim limitations — claim construction and patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim language not tied to specific structure covers all devices capable of performing the recited function; a prior art device that inherently performs the function may support a rejection, but claim construction can narrow a claim to hardware+software where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and guidance: In re Translogic ('coupled to receive' construed as 'capable of receiving'); Intel Corp. (programmable means can be programmed to perform claimed functionality); Nazomi Communications (claims construed to require hardware+software when hardware alone cannot meet limitations); Paulsen (broad 'computer' can encompass calculators). Automation of known functions on a general-purpose computer may be obvious (KSR) and applying routine computer/web technologies can be predictable. Examiners should consider specification support and claim construction to determine whether functional language requires specific structure (hardware, software) or is broad enough to read on prior art devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material or article worked upon does not impart patentability to apparatus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Including the material or article worked upon by a claimed structure does not, by itself, render the apparatus patentable; claim patentability is determined by positive recited structural elements of the apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: In re Otto; In re Young; In re Casey. For claims directed to machinery that works upon an article/material, references to the article without additional structural distinctions do not overcome prior art. Examiners should not treat the worked-upon material as conferring patentability unless the claim positively recites structural features that are novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of novel/nonobvious starting material or end product on obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A process limited to making or using a novel and nonobvious product does not automatically make the process nonobvious; obviousness under §103 requires a fact-specific, whole-invention comparison to prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per In re Ochiai and In re Brouwer, per se rules are improper; a process yielding a novel and nonobvious product may nonetheless be obvious and vice versa. Applicants/Examiners must consider all claim limitations; cases illustrate outcomes both ways (Durden, Albertson, Kanter found obvious; Pleuddemann, Kuehl, Mancy found patentable). Treat language reciting making/using a nonobvious product as a material limitation for claim construction/analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and treatment of Markush claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim recites a list of alternatively useable members (a 'Markush group'); claims reciting alternatively usable members, regardless of format, should be treated as Markush claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Origins: Ex parte Markush; In re Harnisch. Markush groupings commonly appear in chemistry, biology, pharmacology, but can also be used in mechanical/process contexts. Terms like 'selected from the group consisting of' typically indicate a closed group, and 'consisting of' carries a strong presumption of being closed. See MPEP §2111.03 for 'consisting of' treatment and MPEP §803.02 for election/search/examination of claims with Markush groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Markush grouping criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush grouping is improper if the members do not share a single structural similarity or do not share a common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: In re Harnisch and the Supplementary Guidelines. When a Markush group describes part of a combination or process, members following 'selected from the group consisting of' must be substitutable one for the other with the expectation of achieving the same intended result (Multilayer Stretch Cling Film v. Berry Plastics). For chemical compound Markush groups, members need not share properties individually; propriety is determined by the compound as a whole. Examiners should analyze structural similarity and common use (see subsections II–IV of MPEP §2117).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitutability and common use standards for Markush groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a Markush grouping describes part of a combination or process, alternatives must be substitutable with an expectation the same result will be achieved; for chemical compounds, the compound as a whole determines propriety even if individual members differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in a combination/process context, alternatives must be functionally equivalent in the context of the claimed invention. For chemical compounds recited as part of a compound, the propriety of grouping is based on considering each alternative compound as a whole (In re Harnisch, In re Jones). Examiners should determine whether members are members of a recognized class or share an essential structural feature that supports a common use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single structural similarity standard for Markush groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of a Markush group share a 'single structural similarity' when they belong to the same recognized physical/chemical/art-recognized class such that members are expected to behave similarly in the claimed context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recognized class is one where art knowledge gives an expectation members will behave the same in the claimed invention (e.g., diaper fasteners that are known to be substitutable). Where a Markush group includes only members from a recognized class, the existence of the group may itself evidence equivalence and, if one member is anticipated, the group may be rendered unpatentable absent convincing evidence of non-equivalency (In re Ruff). Examiners should assess whether the group members belong to such recognized classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common use derived from substantial structural feature in Markush claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When alternative compounds do not obviously belong to a recognized class, they may still be proper Markush members if they share a substantial structural feature essential to a common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If compounds share a substantial structural feature that is essential to achieving the claimed function, that structural commonality can support the propriety of the Markush grouping (Ex parte Hozumi). The examiner should look for disclosure in the specification or art evidence that the members are functionally equivalent or share the necessary structural feature for the claimed use.
